source: Written for Wayword as a learner's guide; not part of the original dataset. Examples are dataset phrases.
intro: Italian is pronounced almost exactly as it's written. The two things to train are double consonants and the c/g rules.
reading: CAPITALS mark the stress, usually on the second-to-last syllable.
Every vowel is said, including the last one: per favore ends in a clear "eh".
Doubled letters in the pronunciation (kahf-FEH, vor-RAY) mean hold the consonant.

sounds.name: Double consonants
sounds.how: Hold a doubled consonant for longer, with a tiny pause before releasing it. The difference changes meaning (pala/palla, caro/carro).

sounds.name: Soft C and G
sounds.how: Before i or e, c = ch and g = j. The i is often just a spelling signal: ciao is "chow", giorno is "JOR-noh".

sounds.name: Hard C and G
sounds.how: Adding an h keeps them hard: chi is "kee", che is "keh".

sounds.name: GN and GLI
sounds.how: gn = ny as in "canyon" (bagno is "BAH-nyoh"). gli = a soft ly, like the lli in "million".

sounds.name: SC
sounds.how: Before i or e, sc = sh (lascia is "LAH-shah"). Before other vowels it's sk (capisco).

sounds.name: Z
sounds.how: z is ts (grazie is "GRAH-tsyeh"), or dz in some words. It's never the English z.

sounds.name: Rolled R
sounds.how: A tap, or a short trill, with the tip of the tongue. A double rr is a full trill.
